```{=html}
<div class="page page-article reveal">
  <a href="../insights.html" class="arrow-link article-back">← Insights</a>

  <div class="eyebrow page-eyebrow">Data Engineering · Build</div>
  <h1 class="page-title">Don't load what failed</h1>
  <p class="article-deck">
    I built an ETL pipeline for public FRED data — unemployment, GDP, and the 10-year
    Treasury yield. The extract is ordinary. The point is the gate: a series that fails
    schema, continuity, range, or duplicate checks is written to a QA report and
    <em>never enters the database</em>.
  </p>

  <dl class="article-meta">
    <div><dt>Role</dt><dd>Builder</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Case</dt><dd>FRED economic-data ETL</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Stack</dt><dd>Python · pandas · DuckDB · pytest</dd></div>
    <div><dt>Date</dt><dd>September 20, 2026</dd></div>
  </dl>
  <p><a href="https://github.com/eeshajagdhane/public-data-etl-pipeline" class="arrow-link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">View on GitHub →</a></p>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The problem</h2>
    <p>Dashboards inherit whatever you feed them. A silent schema change, a stretch of
    missing dates, a duplicated observation, or a value with the decimal in the wrong
    place will not announce itself. It will just sit in every chart downstream.</p>
    <p>I wanted a pipeline where that cannot happen quietly. Three public FRED series
    go in. Five data-quality checks run. Only series that pass every check are upserted
    into DuckDB. Failures still produce a timestamped markdown report — they just do
    not become “official” rows.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-stats">
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">3</div><div class="article-stat-l">FRED series</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">5</div><div class="article-stat-l">Quality checks per series</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">0</div><div class="article-stat-l">Failed series loaded</div></div>
    <div class="article-stat"><div class="article-stat-v">"." → NaN</div><div class="article-stat-l">FRED's missing marker</div></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What gets pulled</h2>
    <p>The series are deliberately different cadences, because continuity is not one
    number. Monthly unemployment, quarterly GDP, and a daily Treasury yield each need
    their own idea of “too large a gap.”</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-tbl-wrap">
    <table class="article-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Series</th><th>What it is</th><th>Frequency</th><th>Max gap</th><th>Plausible range</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>UNRATE</td><td>Civilian unemployment rate</td><td>Monthly</td><td>45 days</td><td>0 to 50%</td></tr>
        <tr><td>GDP</td><td>Gross domestic product</td><td>Quarterly</td><td>100 days</td><td>0 to $1,000,000B</td></tr>
        <tr><td>DGS10</td><td>10-year Treasury yield</td><td>Daily</td><td>4 days</td><td>−5 to 25%</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
  <p class="article-fine">Ranges are wide plausibility bounds, not forecasts. Their job is to catch a negative unemployment rate or a misplaced decimal, not to predict next quarter.</p>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Five checks, one gate</h2>
    <p>Each series is tested independently. The series as a whole loads only if every
    check returns pass. Select a check to see what it actually asks.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">What each check allows</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">The interesting design is not “flag nulls.” It is which nulls are allowed.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-seg" role="group" aria-label="Quality check">
      <button id="c-schema" aria-pressed="true">Schema</button>
      <button id="c-null" aria-pressed="false">Nulls</button>
      <button id="c-gap" aria-pressed="false">Continuity</button>
      <button id="c-range" aria-pressed="false">Range</button>
      <button id="c-dup" aria-pressed="false">Duplicates</button>
    </div>
    <div class="article-qout" id="cout"></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>Break a series and watch the gate</h2>
    <p>This is the decision the pipeline makes, using the same rules as the tests.
    A missing <em>value</em> is FRED being honest. A missing <em>date</em> is a broken
    identity. Only one of those is allowed through.</p>
  </section>

  <div class="article-panel">
    <div class="article-panel-head">
      <div>
        <div class="article-panel-title">Should this series load?</div>
        <div class="article-panel-sub">Pick a defect. The five checks run; the load decision follows.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="article-seg" role="group" aria-label="Defect">
      <button id="d-clean" aria-pressed="true">Clean monthly</button>
      <button id="d-vnull" aria-pressed="false">Null value</button>
      <button id="d-dnull" aria-pressed="false">Null date</button>
      <button id="d-gap" aria-pressed="false">90-day gap</button>
      <button id="d-range" aria-pressed="false">UNRATE = 999</button>
      <button id="d-dup" aria-pressed="false">Duplicate row</button>
    </div>
    <div class="ledger" id="ledger"></div>
    <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>
  </div>

  <section class="article-section">
    <div class="article-callout">
      <p>FRED encodes a missing observation as the character <strong>"."</strong>. The
      transform turns that into NaN before any check runs. If I had treated every null
      as a failure, every Treasury series would fail on market holidays. The null check
      fails only on <code>date</code> and <code>series_id</code> — the columns that
      identify a row. Value nulls are counted and reported, then passed.</p>
    </div>
    <p>Daily continuity uses a <strong>4-day</strong> threshold so Friday-to-Monday
    (3 days) is not an outage, while a real multi-day hole is. Holidays still appear
    as null-valued rows, which the null check already sees. Two different absences,
    two different checks.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What happens after a pass</h2>
    <p>Validated rows are upserted into DuckDB on the primary key
    <code>(date, series_id)</code>. Re-running the pipeline updates existing
    observations in place instead of stacking duplicates. Raw JSON is saved
    untouched in <code>data/raw/</code> so transform and validate can be replayed
    without hitting the API again.</p>
    <p>A failed series still writes to the QA report. The failure is auditable.
    It is just not in the table a dashboard would read.</p>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>The technical layer</h2>
    <div class="article-tech-label">For readers who want the mechanics</div>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>Why transform is a pure function</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Extract talks to the network. Load talks to disk. Transform takes a decoded
    JSON payload and a series ID and returns a three-column DataFrame —
    <code>date</code>, <code>series_id</code>, <code>value</code> — with no I/O.
    That is what makes the JSON-to-table logic unit-testable with fixtures instead
    of a live FRED key.</p>
    <p>FRED does not stamp <code>series_id</code> onto each observation. The caller
    that requested the series has to pass it in. Forgetting that would produce a
    table of anonymous dates, so the transform is also where identity is attached.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>The load rule in one line</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>For each series: extract, transform, validate. Then:</p>
    <p><strong>if every check passed → upsert; else → log the failed check names and skip.</strong></p>
    <p>The QA report is written either way. The database is not. That split is the
    whole project. A dashboard that reads DuckDB is reading only series that cleared
    the gate on that run.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What the tests actually pin down</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p>Each check has a passing case and a failing case. Schema fails on a missing
    column or a string-typed <code>value</code>. Nulls pass when only <code>value</code>
    is empty, and fail when <code>date</code> is. Continuity fails if two monthly
    points are January and April (a gap over 45 days). Range fails at 999 against a
    max of 50. Duplicates fail when the same <code>(date, series_id)</code> appears
    twice. Range ignores NaN, so a holiday is not an out-of-range event.</p>
    <p>Those fixtures are the spec. The interactive panel above is the same logic
    with the numbers filled in.</p>
    </div>
    </details>

    <details class="article-details">
    <summary>What I'd do differently</summary>
    <div class="article-det-body">
    <p><strong>Fail a row, not always a whole series.</strong> Today one out-of-range
    point blocks the entire series from loading. That is conservative and correct
    for a first gate. A production version would quarantine the bad rows and load
    the rest, with the report naming which dates were held back.</p>
    <p><strong>Tighten ranges once I have a history of observed maxima.</strong> The
    current bounds are “this cannot be real,” not “this is unusual.” Unusual is a
    different check — a z-score or a month-over-month jump — and it belongs in a
    second pass, not in the plausibility gate.</p>
    <p><strong>Run it on a schedule.</strong> The upsert is already idempotent. The
    missing piece is treating each run as a freshness SLA: if UNRATE has not moved
    in 45 days, that is a continuity failure worth paging, not just a report line.</p>
    </div>
    </details>
  </section>

  <section class="article-section">
    <h2>What this case taught me</h2>
    <p><strong>ETL is extract, transform, validate, then maybe load.</strong> Writing
    everything that parsed is how bad data becomes a dashboard. The validation step
    is only a gate if load is allowed to refuse.</p>
    <p><strong>Not every missing value is the same missing.</strong> A null date
    breaks the key. A null yield on a market holiday is the source telling the
    truth. Collapsing those into one “null check” would either fail every daily
    series or accept broken identities.</p>
    <p><strong>A bound is a cheaper alarm than a model.</strong> Unemployment cannot
    be 999. A 90-day hole in a monthly series is not a weekend. Those are the same
    kind of ceiling I used on campaign profit: if a number is past what the world
    allows, stop promoting it.</p>
    <div class="chips article-chips">
      <span class="chip">ETL</span>
      <span class="chip">Data quality</span>
      <span class="chip">FRED API</span>
      <span class="chip">DuckDB</span>
      <span class="chip">pytest</span>
      <span class="chip">Schema validation</span>
      <span class="chip">Python</span>
    </div>
    <p class="article-fine">Figures and rules are from my pipeline on public FRED series.
    The data source is the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. No API keys are stored
    in the repository.</p>
  </section>
</div>
</main>

<script>
  const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
    entries.forEach(e => { if (e.isIntersecting) e.target.classList.add('visible'); });
  }, { threshold: 0.08 });
  document.querySelectorAll('.reveal').forEach(el => io.observe(el));

  (function(){
    var CHECKS={
      schema:{t:"Schema",
        b:"Columns must be date (datetime), series_id (string), value (float). A missing column or a value stored as text fails. This is the check that catches a silent API shape change before it becomes a table of strings."},
      null:{t:"Nulls",
        b:"Nulls in date or series_id fail — those columns are the identity of a row. Nulls in value pass, and the report records the count and percentage. FRED's \".\" placeholder is already NaN by this point, so a holiday is reported, not rejected."},
      gap:{t:"Date continuity",
        b:"Sort the dates and measure the gap to the next one. Daily allows 4 days (weekends pass; a real outage does not). Monthly allows 45. Quarterly allows 100. Unknown frequencies fail, because there is no honest threshold."},
      range:{t:"Range",
        b:"Non-null values must sit inside a wide plausibility band. Unemployment 0–50, yields −5–25, GDP at least zero. NaNs are ignored so a missing observation is not an out-of-range event. 999% unemployment fails. 14% does not."},
      dup:{t:"Duplicates",
        b:"The grain is (date, series_id). Two rows with the same pair fail. The load step later upserts on that same key — so if duplicates got through, the primary key would be lying about uniqueness."}
    };
    var order=["schema","null","gap","range","dup"];
    var cout=document.getElementById("cout");
    function show(id){
      order.forEach(function(k){
        document.getElementById("c-"+k).setAttribute("aria-pressed", k===id);
      });
      var c=CHECKS[id];
      cout.innerHTML="<strong>"+c.t+".</strong> "+c.b;
    }
    order.forEach(function(k){
      document.getElementById("c-"+k).addEventListener("click",function(){show(k);});
    });
    show("schema");

    var DEFS={
      clean:{label:"Clean monthly UNRATE",
        rows:[
          {n:"schema",ok:true,d:"date / series_id / value with correct types"},
          {n:"null",ok:true,d:"no null keys; 0% value nulls"},
          {n:"date_continuity",ok:true,d:"monthly gaps under 45 days"},
          {n:"range",ok:true,d:"values inside [0, 50]"},
          {n:"duplicate",ok:true,d:"unique (date, series_id)"}
        ]},
      vnull:{label:"One missing unemployment print",
        rows:[
          {n:"schema",ok:true,d:"shape unchanged"},
          {n:"null",ok:true,d:"value nulls: 1 (25%). Keys intact — pass, and report it"},
          {n:"date_continuity",ok:true,d:"dates still monthly"},
          {n:"range",ok:true,d:"NaN ignored by the range check"},
          {n:"duplicate",ok:true,d:"still unique keys"}
        ]},
      dnull:{label:"Null date on a row",
        rows:[
          {n:"schema",ok:true,d:"columns present"},
          {n:"null",ok:false,d:"unexpected nulls in key columns: date=1"},
          {n:"date_continuity",ok:true,d:"remaining dates still regular"},
          {n:"range",ok:true,d:"values in range"},
          {n:"duplicate",ok:true,d:"keys unique among non-null dates"}
        ]},
      gap:{label:"January, then April — two months dropped",
        rows:[
          {n:"schema",ok:true,d:"columns present"},
          {n:"null",ok:true,d:"keys intact"},
          {n:"date_continuity",ok:false,d:"1 gap exceeds 45d for monthly (≈90d)"},
          {n:"range",ok:true,d:"values in range"},
          {n:"duplicate",ok:true,d:"keys unique"}
        ]},
      range:{label:"UNRATE printed as 999",
        rows:[
          {n:"schema",ok:true,d:"value is still a float"},
          {n:"null",ok:true,d:"keys intact"},
          {n:"date_continuity",ok:true,d:"dates monthly"},
          {n:"range",ok:false,d:"1 value outside [0, 50]. Example: 999"},
          {n:"duplicate",ok:true,d:"keys unique"}
        ]},
      dup:{label:"Same date ingested twice",
        rows:[
          {n:"schema",ok:true,d:"columns present"},
          {n:"null",ok:true,d:"keys intact"},
          {n:"date_continuity",ok:true,d:"distinct dates still monthly"},
          {n:"range",ok:true,d:"values in range"},
          {n:"duplicate",ok:false,d:"2 duplicate (date, series_id) rows"}
        ]}
    };
    var dorder=["clean","vnull","dnull","gap","range","dup"];
    var led=document.getElementById("ledger"), vd=document.getElementById("verdict");
    function render(id){
      dorder.forEach(function(k){
        document.getElementById("d-"+k).setAttribute("aria-pressed", k===id);
      });
      var s=DEFS[id], html="", pass=true;
      s.rows.forEach(function(r){
        if(!r.ok) pass=false;
        html+="<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k'>"+r.n+"</span><span class='led-v'>"+
          (r.ok?"pass":"fail")+"</span></div>";
        html+="<div class='led-row'><span class='led-k' style='font-weight:400;color:var(--ink-mute)'>"+
          r.d+"</span><span class='led-v'></span></div>";
      });
      html+="<div class='led-row tot'><span>Load into DuckDB?</span><span class='led-v'>"+
        (pass?"yes":"no")+"</span></div>";
      led.innerHTML=html;
      vd.innerHTML=pass
        ? "<span class='badge yes'>Load</span><br>Every check passed. <strong>"+s.label+"</strong> is upserted and the QA report marks PASS."
        : "<span class='badge no'>Skip</span><br><strong>"+s.label+"</strong> is written to the QA report and <em>not</em> loaded. The dashboard never sees it.";
    }
    dorder.forEach(function(k){
      document.getElementById("d-"+k).addEventListener("click",function(){render(k);});
    });
    render("clean");
  })();
</script>
```
